# Results

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Plain-Language Summary
This section presents the final **de-leaked** performance of the two leading
backbones in detail. The headline result is that removing description leakage
**reversed the backbone ranking**: Clinical ModernBERT (E-024) reaches 76.9%
end-to-end accuracy and 73.7% auto-coding at 90.0% precision, beating
ClinicalBERT (E-021, 59.2%) — the opposite of what the leaky benchmark showed.
:::

---

## Overall Performance {#sec-results-overall}

All metrics below are computed on the **de-leaked** gold data, on a single
content-addressed held-out test set of 966 billable-code records (the same
test partition for every model, so comparisons are exact). Metrics are
reported after temperature-scaling calibration.

The de-leaked best model is **E-024 (Clinical ModernBERT)**. ClinicalBERT
(E-021) — the winner on the leaky benchmark — is shown alongside it.

| Metric | E-024 ModernBERT | E-021 ClinicalBERT | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top-1 (E2E) accuracy | **76.9%** | 59.2% | 743 vs 572 of 966 correct |
| Macro F1 | **0.672** | 0.477 | Unweighted mean F1 across codes |
| Stage-1 routing accuracy | 95.3% | 95.6% | Routers near-identical — leakage did not affect routing |
| Within-chapter accuracy | **80.7%** | 62.0% | Among correctly routed records |
| ECE (post-calibration) | **0.039** | 0.088 | Expected Calibration Error — lower is better |
| Coverage@0.7 | **73.7%** | 55.3% | Fraction auto-coded at τ=0.7 |
| Accuracy on auto-coded | **90.0%** | 83.7% | Precision on covered cases |

: De-leaked evaluation results, E-024 vs E-021. {#tbl-results-overall}

The two Stage-1 routers are essentially identical (95.3% vs 95.6%), which
localises the entire backbone difference to **Stage-2 within-chapter
resolution** (80.7% vs 62.0%). Chapter routing barely depends on the leaked
descriptions; the within-chapter code choice is where the leaked signal — and
the architectural difference — lives.

### Error Analysis

Errors are overwhelmingly within-chapter for both models, confirming that the
router is not the bottleneck:

| | E-024 ModernBERT | E-021 ClinicalBERT |
|---|---|---|
| Total errors | 223 / 966 | 394 / 966 |
| Within-chapter (right chapter, wrong code) | 178 (80%) | 351 (89%) |
| Cross-chapter (wrong chapter) | 45 (20%) | 43 (11%) |

ModernBERT makes far fewer total errors (223 vs 394). For both models, the
large majority of errors are within-chapter — the Stage-1 router sends the
note to the right chapter, but the Stage-2 resolver picks the wrong specific
code. Improvements to within-chapter resolution therefore have more headroom
than further router improvements.

---

## Per-Chapter Results — the Inversion {#sec-results-chapter}

The per-chapter breakdown is the clearest evidence that the backbone reversal
is **architectural rather than an artifact of one leaky chapter**. Clinical
ModernBERT beats ClinicalBERT in **17 of 19 chapters**, with broadly
distributed margins (+0.09 to +0.36) rather than a gain concentrated in one
or two chapters. The two exceptions (A, B) are tiny-sample chapters (n=6, 16).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-results-chapter
#| tbl-cap: "Per-chapter E2E accuracy, de-leaked: Clinical ModernBERT (E-024) vs ClinicalBERT (E-021), same 966-record test set. ModernBERT wins 17/19 chapters."

import pandas as pd

chapter_results = [
    {"Chapter": "A", "Description": "Infectious diseases", "n": 6,   "ModernBERT": "16.7%", "ClinicalBERT": "33.3%", "Δ": "-0.167", "Note": "n=6 — noise"},
    {"Chapter": "B", "Description": "Viral infections",    "n": 16,  "ModernBERT": "68.8%", "ClinicalBERT": "68.8%", "Δ": "+0.000", "Note": "tie (n=16)"},
    {"Chapter": "C", "Description": "Neoplasms",           "n": 51,  "ModernBERT": "76.5%", "ClinicalBERT": "58.8%", "Δ": "+0.177", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "D", "Description": "Blood diseases",      "n": 38,  "ModernBERT": "84.2%", "ClinicalBERT": "60.5%", "Δ": "+0.237", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "E", "Description": "Endocrine/metabolic", "n": 39,  "ModernBERT": "76.9%", "ClinicalBERT": "51.3%", "Δ": "+0.256", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "F", "Description": "Mental disorders",    "n": 48,  "ModernBERT": "70.8%", "ClinicalBERT": "43.8%", "Δ": "+0.271", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "G", "Description": "Nervous system",      "n": 34,  "ModernBERT": "73.5%", "ClinicalBERT": "64.7%", "Δ": "+0.088", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "H", "Description": "Eye/ear",             "n": 42,  "ModernBERT": "78.6%", "ClinicalBERT": "76.2%", "Δ": "+0.024", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "I", "Description": "Circulatory",         "n": 66,  "ModernBERT": "74.2%", "ClinicalBERT": "51.5%", "Δ": "+0.227", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "J", "Description": "Respiratory",         "n": 50,  "ModernBERT": "74.0%", "ClinicalBERT": "38.0%", "Δ": "+0.360", "Note": "largest gap"},
    {"Chapter": "K", "Description": "Digestive",           "n": 58,  "ModernBERT": "87.9%", "ClinicalBERT": "70.7%", "Δ": "+0.172", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "L", "Description": "Skin",                "n": 38,  "ModernBERT": "94.7%", "ClinicalBERT": "65.8%", "Δ": "+0.289", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "M", "Description": "Musculoskeletal",     "n": 111, "ModernBERT": "70.3%", "ClinicalBERT": "53.1%", "Δ": "+0.171", "Note": "largest chapter"},
    {"Chapter": "N", "Description": "Genitourinary",       "n": 53,  "ModernBERT": "84.9%", "ClinicalBERT": "62.3%", "Δ": "+0.226", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "O", "Description": "Pregnancy",           "n": 32,  "ModernBERT": "78.1%", "ClinicalBERT": "59.4%", "Δ": "+0.187", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "R", "Description": "Symptoms/signs",      "n": 100, "ModernBERT": "80.0%", "ClinicalBERT": "66.0%", "Δ": "+0.140", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "S", "Description": "Injuries",            "n": 44,  "ModernBERT": "81.8%", "ClinicalBERT": "79.5%", "Δ": "+0.023", "Note": ""},
    {"Chapter": "T", "Description": "Poisoning/effects",   "n": 8,   "ModernBERT": "100%",  "ClinicalBERT": "75.0%", "Δ": "+0.250", "Note": "n=8 — noise"},
    {"Chapter": "Z", "Description": "Administrative",      "n": 132, "ModernBERT": "70.5%", "ClinicalBERT": "56.1%", "Δ": "+0.144", "Note": "largest chapter"},
]

df = pd.DataFrame(chapter_results)
from IPython.display import Markdown
display(Markdown(df.to_markdown(index=False)))
```

### Chapter Analysis

**The gain is broad, not localised.** ModernBERT's advantage spans nearly
every well-sampled chapter — from +0.14 (Z, R) through +0.36 (J, respiratory).
If the reversal were caused by residual leakage surviving in a particular
chapter, we would expect the gain to concentrate there; instead it is spread
across the whole code space, which is the signature of a genuinely stronger
backbone rather than a localised data artifact.

**The two exceptions are noise, not counter-evidence.** Chapter A (n=6) and
chapter B (n=16) are the only chapters where ModernBERT does not win, and both
are too small to support any conclusion — a single record swings chapter A by
16.7 points.

**The Z (administrative) chapter remains relatively hard for both** (70.5% /
56.1%). Its 263 codes cover screening, follow-up, and administrative contacts
whose notes are linguistically similar across codes. This is the chapter the
leaky benchmark claimed SupCon "solved" (+21.2pp); de-leaked, that gain almost
entirely disappears (see @sec-results-comparison and the experiments section).

---

## Calibration Analysis {#sec-results-calibration}

Calibration quality underpins confidence-gating: if confidence scores do not
track accuracy, the τ=0.7 threshold cannot be trusted.

Both de-leaked models calibrate well after temperature scaling, with
ModernBERT notably better calibrated (ECE 0.039) than ClinicalBERT (0.088).
The better calibration is consistent with ModernBERT's higher and more
reliable accuracy — it is not merely more accurate but more honest about when
it is uncertain.

---

## Selective Automation Analysis {#sec-results-automation}

The confidence-gating mechanism enables a deployment mode that auto-codes
high-confidence cases and defers uncertain ones. The de-leaked coverage-accuracy
tradeoff is shown below for both models.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-results-automation
#| tbl-cap: "De-leaked coverage-accuracy tradeoff at varying confidence thresholds. ModernBERT dominates ClinicalBERT on BOTH coverage and precision at every threshold."

import pandas as pd

rows = [
    {"τ": 0.5,  "MB coverage": "83.8%", "MB acc": "86.7%", "CB coverage": "69.5%", "CB acc": "76.8%"},
    {"τ": 0.6,  "MB coverage": "78.2%", "MB acc": "89.3%", "CB coverage": "61.1%", "CB acc": "81.0%"},
    {"τ": "**0.7**", "MB coverage": "**73.7%**", "MB acc": "**90.0%**", "CB coverage": "**55.3%**", "CB acc": "**83.7%**"},
    {"τ": 0.8,  "MB coverage": "66.6%", "MB acc": "92.5%", "CB coverage": "47.6%", "CB acc": "86.3%"},
]

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
from IPython.display import Markdown
display(Markdown(df.to_markdown(index=False)))
```

A key observation: ModernBERT is better on **both** axes at every threshold —
higher coverage *and* higher precision. The backbone choice is not a
coverage/precision tradeoff; ModernBERT simply dominates. At τ=0.7 it
auto-codes 73.7% of cases at 90.0% precision, versus ClinicalBERT's 55.3% at
83.7%.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Operational Interpretation (de-leaked, ModernBERT)

At τ=0.7, a department processing 1,000 notes per day using the de-leaked
ModernBERT model would auto-code ~737 notes at ~90% precision (~74 errors for
retrospective correction) and route ~263 to human coders. This is a more
modest automation profile than the leaky figures implied — but it rests on
data that does not leak the answer, so it is a defensible estimate rather than
an inflated one.
:::

## Comparison with Previous Approaches {#sec-results-comparison}

| Approach | E2E Accuracy | Macro F1 | ECE | Coverage@0.7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **E-024 Clinical ModernBERT (de-leaked best)** | **76.9%** | **0.672** | **0.039** | **73.7%** |
| E-021 ClinicalBERT (de-leaked) | 59.2% | 0.477 | 0.088 | 55.3% |
| E-022 ClinicalBERT + SupCon Z (de-leaked) | 59.7% | — | 0.089 | 56.1% |
| E-026 BioClinical ModernBERT (de-leaked) | 39.8% | 0.289 | 0.049 | 18.3% |

: De-leaked comparison across configurations. {#tbl-results-comparison}

Two points stand out. First, **SupCon adds only +0.5pp** at the system level
(59.2%→59.7%) on de-leaked data — the leaky benchmark's +21.2pp Z-chapter gain
was overwhelmingly leakage, not contrastive learning. Second, the two
ModernBERT variants bracket the range: Clinical ModernBERT is the strongest
backbone tested, while BioClinical ModernBERT is the weakest — architecture
family alone does not determine performance, the specific pretraining does.

::: {.callout-note}
## On the leaky-regime numbers
The previously reported figures (E-010 at 85.8%, the E-005c/Graph/Override
comparison, the +21.2pp SupCon result) were all measured on data that leaked
diagnostic descriptions into the note text. They are not reproduced here as
valid results; the experiments section documents the discrepancy in full.
:::
